messages.body_plain:
So this is my ad hoc-ish solution using existing secr functions. It's not tidied up as yet so I've just directly entered population and detection parameters into the functions inside the function.

data_sim <- function(){
  success <- FALSE
  while(!success){
    pop_f <- sim.popn(D = 0.2,
                      core = grid_traps,
                      buffer = 100,
                      poly = land, # drops ACs that fall in water
                      nsessions = 10,
                      covariates = list(sex = c(M = 0,
                                                F = 1)),
                      Ndist = "fixed",
                      details = list(phi = 0.9,
                                     lambda = 2.3,
                                     movemodel = "exponential",
                                     move.a = 5,
                                     edgemethod = "reflect")) # if ACs hit the edge of the island they move back in
    # to keep population size within a reasonable range
    success <- 55 <= dim(pop_f[[10]])[1] & dim(pop_f[[10]])[1] <= 80
  }
  success <- FALSE
  while(!success){
    pop_m <- sim.popn(D = 0.2,
                      core = grid_traps,
                      buffer = 100,
                      poly = land, # drops ACs that fall in water
                      nsessions = 10,
                      covariates = list(sex = c(M = 1,
                                                F = 0)),
                      Ndist = "fixed",
                      details = list(phi = 0.9,
                                     lambda = 2.3,
                                     movemodel = "exponential",
                                     move.a = 5,
                                     edgemethod = "reflect")) # if ACs hit the edge of the island they move back in
    # to keep population size within a reasonable range
    success <- 55 <= dim(pop_m[[10]])[1] & dim(pop_m[[10]])[1] <= 80
  }
  # females
  ch_f_grid <- sim.capthist(traps = grid_traps,
                            popn = pop_f,
                            noccasions = 4,
                            detectfn = "EX",
                            detectpar = list(g0 = 0.2,
                                             sigma = 40),
                            nsessions = 10,
                            renumber = FALSE)
  # males
  ch_m_grid <- sim.capthist(traps = grid_traps,
                            popn = pop_m,
                            noccasions = 4,
                            detectfn = "EX",
                            detectpar = list(g0 = 0.3,
                                             sigma = 80),
                            nsessions = 10,
                            renumber = FALSE)
  # bind capthists together
  ch_grid <- list()
  for(s in 1:10){
    ch_grid[[s]] <- rbind(ch_f_grid[[s]],
                          ch_m_grid[[s]])
  }
  return(list(ch_grid, pop_f, pop_m))
}

'grid_traps' and 'land' attached. I'm trying to use simulations to verify our inferences in a high trap saturation scenario.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using SECR 4.2 to estimate the population density of fishers in central BC and have run into a few issues when attempting to fit more complex models to my dataset (capthist summary below).

> summary(ChilcotinCH)

Object class       capthist

Detector type      proximity

Detector number    256

Average spacing    1594.814 m

x-range            379687 469516 m

y-range            5779995 5819202 m

 Usage range by occasion

    1 2 3 4

min 0 0 0 0

max 1 1 1 1

Counts by occasion

                    1   2   3   4 Total

n                  20  26  26  24    96

u                  20  13  11   4    48

f                  18  19   4   7    48

M(t+1)             20  33  44  48    48

losses              0   0   0   0     0

detections         21  37  35  34   127

detectors visited  21  37  35  34   127

detectors used    113 120 122 120   475

So, my general work flow was to generate my habitat mask and fit the null model ---> determine the top observation model by using different combinations of the built-in models in SECR 4.2 ) --->  do some density surface modelling to determine which habitat covariates in my habitat mask are the most influential --->  specify more complex models using different combinations of the top observation model and highest AIC-ranking state models.

The last step is where I have been running into issues, namely failure to converge (either Warning: nlm returned code 4, or Optim returned convergence 1) due to the maximum iteration limit being exceeded. I know my habitat mask is right at the top end for the recommended number of points (over in fact, at 2,129), which has not been an issue up until this last step. I have attempted to use the starting value of a previously successfully fit model, as well as using the more robust ‘Nelder-Mead’ method, neither of which has seemed to help.

When I went back and explored the top ranked observation model (g0 ~ Bk, sigma ~ Bk) more closely, I noticed that the estimated g0 for this model was actually 1, which has made me quite suspicious of its validity. I have begun using the next highest ranked observation model (g0 ~ Bk, sigma ~ 1) during the last step of my workflow, and this has eliminated the convergence issues I was seeing when using the top ranked observation model.

So I guess my questions are as follows:

1.      Has anyone run into the same issues when using models where g0 and sigma both change with respect to Bk, either with failing to converge and/or a g0 of 1?

2.      Given the suspiciousness of an estimated detection probability of 1, would it be valid to drop this model and use the next best observation model instead?

Happy to provide more details, sample code, etc, but thought I would start with these more general questions first. Apologies if there is something obvious I have missed, but any insight would be greatly appreciated. Thanks!

Rory

Dear Eric and Murray,

I was looking for answers to similar questions that I had for my study. I followed the thread and wanted to check if I am using the correct approach.
We had camera traps at 10 sites for sampling snow leopard population for a large region (Indian state). We used multisession models (D~session) to compare differences in estimates of D between sites. Now, we are interested in estimating mean densities at the larger spatial scale, using our multisession model (D~session).

I am using derived() to get estimate of D, se, and esa. for each site. From this thread - I am using weighted 'R3' method because they seem to work better (i.e related to overestimation of se) when D varies across the study area. I have 2 clarifications.

1. Can I say  independent.esa = F, because the data is shared between sessions? This is similar to what Eric asked "sets of animals do not overlap, but information is shared when estimating the parameters of the detection function, even if I include (additive) session effects".

2. From the output of the derived(), can I calculate an average density across sites from (D~session) model for the whole state, and get confidence limits via the delta method?

3. Generally speaking, when there is heterogeneity in densities over space, is it better to use meaningful spatial covariate models to estimate densities (by taking average of predicted density surfaces), because they can use a inhomogeneous Poisson model?

This conversation thread was very helpful. Thanks!

Best,
Manvi

If home ranges are bivariate normals, the 95% home range radius is r = sqrt(5.99) * sigma. Then, the area of a circle is A = pi * r^2. So a sigma of 32 km yields a 95% home range size of 19270 km^2, nearly 3x larger than the home range size estimate you provided. If sigma was actually 6 km, you would get a 95% home range area of 677 km^2, in line with your estimate. I believe sigma is not identifiable given this trapping array, at least using an isotropic detection function.

Because animal movement is elongated along the major axis of the trapping array and the array is too narrow to encompass individual movement along the minor axis, it is possible that sigma might be identifiable under the anisotropic detection function model, but not the isotropic detection function model. I can't say I understand why the sigma estimates would go down when increasing the state space extent, but this should be further evidence that sigma is not identifiable and they are still much too large, I believe. I don't think this is a solvable problem with the data in hand unless you are comfortable switching to a Bayesian analysis and using an informative prior for sigma, which isn't ideal because your inference depends on the accuracy of your sigma prior. In a perfect world, you could go deploy a larger trapping array, but I know that is likely not an option.

I like Murray's advice further up in this conversation:

For decision makers: "We photographed 8 different leopards in 2012 and 5 in 2016, and know quite a lot about these individuals. However, we are unable to apply the methods of statistical ecology to extrapolate from these known animals to the number and distribution of undetected leopards, and hence to estimate the total population. This is because the numbers are small, the scale of individual movements was large relative to the area we surveyed, the topography constrained sampling and movements preventing us from reliably extrapolating to a 2-dimensional area, etc. Fancy modelling cannot change these fundamentals."

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I am using the Royle and Young 2008 SCR model paired with Efford's 2011 MLE expansion to explore density estimates for the flat-tailed horned lizard using area search. I want to know how parameter estimates are affected by addition of variable amounts of telemetry data, so I am pairing the capture history and telemetry data, but have stalled with errors that I think must have to do with the mask or discretization of the polygon.

I manually entered the polygon as:

YDMA2Manual <- make.poly (polylist = NULL, x = c(727600 ,727900,727900,727600 ),
                          y = c(3592700, 3592700, 3593000, 3593000 ), exclusive
                          = FALSE, verify = TRUE)

YDMA21_<-read.csv("YDMA21DemoAdjust.csv")

CAPTHIST21<-make.capthist(YDMA21_, YDMA2Manual, fmt="XY")

YDMA21.fit<- secr.fit(CAPTHIST21)
YDMA21.fit

Tele11<-read.csv("Telemetry11.csv")
Tele11_ <- Tele11[, c("Session","Telemetry.ID","Occasion","Easting","Northing")]

Telemetry11 <- read.telemetry(data = Tele11_)
TeleCH21<- MS.capthist(CAPTHIST21,Telemetry11, type = c('independent'))

fit.ms <http://fit.ms> <- secr.fit(TeleCH21, detectfn = 0 , trace = FALSE, verify = FALSE, mask = NULL)

Once I've reached this point I get the error "Error in make.mask(tr, ...) : require spacing for rectangular mask"

Do I need to discretize the polygon, how do I clarify the mask spacing/select a reasonable spacing (the plots are 300m x 300m)?
Thanks so much in advance for your help!

Craig Fischer

One last thought--if your study area is surrounded by non-habitat so close to your trapping array that additional traps cannot be deployed inside habitat, then it sounds like you might be over-buffering your state space as it will include non-habitat. It is possible you could get around sigma not being identifiable by your knowledge of the available habitat. But your results will likely be very sensitive to the accuracy of your delineation of the habitat. Maybe others can chime in about how precarious of an assumption this is.

Ben

I think you're seeing the expected behaviour of predict(): unless you specify levels of 'act' in a dataframe provided by the newdata argument, the reported estimates are for a single, arbitrary level of 'act' (the first, from memory). Note also that covariate models are very slow to fit with secr.fit when there are many levels, so you might be better to bin these.

Murray
